source_integrity.finding: Pending and two complete staged Markdown sources read from main and pinned by Git blob SHA; prior rev6 rejection reviewed.

factual_methodology.finding: 205 contiguous annual entries per language, differentiated events, historical secondary synthesis and interpretation; 1833 qualified; dated 1932, 1969 and 1981; 1997 COP3, 2003 IBSA, 2007 EU summit and efavirenz corrected.

source_vintage_and_cutoff.finding: Historical chronology used as secondary evidence through 2008; official dated materials supplement 2001–2026; 2026 EU interim provisional application distinct from full agreement ratification; Brand Finance 2026 is perception, not outcomes.

research_depth.finding: Long-run 1822–2026 synthesis, 205 annual entries, institutional, economic, social and political mechanisms, comparisons and counterarguments; substantial EN/PT text.

evidence_traceability.finding: Replaced rev6 source mismatches: UNFCCC decision 1/CP.3 for 1997; South African government 6 June 2003 IBSA account; EU Council 11531/07 and Decree 6.108 for 2007. Dated sources for 2001,2005,2006,2008,2009,2011,2012,2013,2016,2022,2023,2025. Annual citations matched across locales.
limitations: Year-indexed Garcia citations are secondary synthesis, not independent primary records; not all 205 historical claims were externally verified line by line.

visual_evidence_readiness.finding: Both locales contain two reproducible additive UN Security Council start-year count charts, [1,2,2,0,1,2,1,1,1] and equal 40-year windows [5,6], with enumerated eleven starts, calculation tables, flow and map; no misleading ordinal bar.

counterfactual_review.finding: Separates attraction from coercion, access from outcomes, cultural visibility from measurable diplomatic effects, event hosting from implementation, and treaty signature from legal application; avoids attributing causal effect of democratization to UN counts.

editorial_publication_readiness.finding: No remaining material rev6 source mismatch detected in targeted source-document checks; English and Portuguese match 205 years, year-linked citations, visual values and analytical qualifications. Approval only, no public promotion.

contrary_evidence: Brand Finance survey measures perceptions and rankings, not causal policy effectiveness or a comparable historical soft-power time series.
Military interventions in the Empire and the peacekeeping mission in Haiti involved coercion, contested local legitimacy and human costs.
Brazil's 2019–2022 diplomatic disagreements did not prevent election to its eleventh Security Council term in 2022–2023.
The 2026 Mercosur–EU provisional trade application is not full definitive ratification of the partnership.
Event hosting at G20, BRICS and COP30 does not establish policy implementation or realized financing.
Brazil's culture can be globally recognizable while political influence remains bounded by veto powers, industrial dependence and domestic institutional credibility.
limitations: Brand Finance index is a proprietary cross-sectional perception instrument; it should not be projected backwards to 1822.
The report does not estimate a synthetic index of historical soft power or an unobservable causal effect of music and sport on diplomatic votes.
Impacts of COP30 decisions, the anti-hunger alliance and Mercosur–EU remain to be verified by future implementation metrics.
News after 11 November 2026 is outside the factual cutoff.
Independent QA, source-hash approval and public site deployment have not yet occurred at producer stage.
Annual entries are historically selective and not an exhaustive documentary inventory; specific terms and negotiations have different certainty levels.

The National Archives imperial chronology is indexed but its original URL has intermittent maintenance redirects; FUNAG, minister appointments and legal primary sources provide accessible cross-checks.
Per-year citations include broad specialist chronologies for some years rather than primary dated instruments; independent QA must still check individual claim-level attribution and may reject.
Sourcing of ministerial appointments does not establish contemporaneous shifts in policy; historical interpretation is separated from the appointment.
The Falklands entry of 1833 distinguishes British seizure and Argentina's objection from later Brazilian diplomatic positions; no unsourced 1833 instrument is alleged.
Signing, ratification and effective application of treaties are separate legal acts; the 1928 Havana and 1948 OAS entries reflect this distinction.
Garcia's published scholarly chronology supplies an indexed historical cross-check for 1822–2008; it is secondary historical synthesis, not 184 independent primary archival investigations.
Not every annual entry corresponds to a diplomatic turning point: dated institutional continuity, domestic constraints and contextual interpretation do not measure realized soft-power effects.
The 2026 perception index is cross-sectional; rankings cannot be extrapolated back into the nineteenth century.

Only a limited sample of Garcia's year-specific historical passages has been verified directly against the full reference PDF; do not infer all 205 annual entries are individually proved merely by hyperlinks.
The 1833 attribution regarding Argentine rights to the Malvinas remains a retrospective scholarly assertion, without independently located contemporaneous dated Brazilian recognition note.
The two charts derive from the same UN 11-term institutional-access series using different aggregation windows and should not be treated as independent observations or effect estimates.
The comparison across two 40-year windows is descriptive and not a causal estimate of democratic transition.
Year citations include multiple official publications and a reference historian; despite revisions, not every interpretive clause has a separate causal identification study.
Revision 7 remains staged and unpublished until independent QA approval with current source and pending blob hashes.
Independent QA externally checked selected critical source passages, not each of the 205 annual claims against primary archives.
Planalto source may deny automated access; legal decree citation retained as official record with alternative legal archives available.
Pipeline command npm run validate:editorial-depth was not executed in a checked-out runtime; deterministic structural checks performed against fetched source files.
notes: Independent editorial QA revision 7. Rev6 blocking source mismatches addressed. Approval is tied to exact source and pending Git blobs; publisher must revalidate and promote separately. No publication asserted.

en.deck: From imperial recognition and Rio Branco to the UN, Mercosur, BRICS, G20 and COP30: why Brazil's cultural visibility exceeds its uneven ability to shape international outcomes.
en.regime: Long-run rise in institutional and cultural visibility, with intermittent geopolitical and economic constraints on effective influence.

watch: Independent diplomacy and climate perception indicators

producer_checks.information_cutoff: As of 2026-11-11 BRT. Brand Finance published 2026-06-12; surveyed more than 150,000 respondents from more than 100 countries; 193 UN member states assessed against 55 metrics. EU–Mercosur signature 2026-01-17 and provisional trade application 2026-05-01 distinguished; 1833 Malvinas recognition is explicitly marked as a retrospective scholarly attribution lacking dated Brazilian dispatch.
producer_checks.source_check: 205 annual entries remain bilingual with year-specific citations. Revision 7 corrects three independent QA mismatches: 1997 links UNFCCC COP3 Kyoto decision 1/CP.3; 2003 links South African government launch of IBSA and Brasilia Declaration June6; 2007 links EU Council joint statement July4 and Brazilian Decree 6108 May4. Additionally replaced 12 broadly or wrongly sourced entries (2001, 2005, 2006, 2008, 2009, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2016, 2022, 2023, 2025) with dated events supported by specific primary/official materials. Additional details of archival source limitations remain acknowledged.
producer_checks.historical_method: Revision 7 deliberately narrows broad interpretive annual claims to checkable source-specific dates and distinguishes signed treaties from effective entry into force, event hosting from outcomes, and roles without veto from realized influence. Garcia year-organized scholarly chronology complements—not substitutes for—official primary material.
producer_checks.argument_continuity: Historical phases compare visibility, attraction, access and demonstrated influence; separates colonial/imperia coercion from later soft power, democratic legitimacy from pragmatic autonomy, climate summits from achieved implementation, and culture from market and diplomacy outcomes.
producer_checks.visual_evidence: Two quantitative charts in EN/PT now both use additive COUNT data from official UN historical membership list: first 11 mandate starts by decade [1,2,2,0,1,2,1,1,1], second same 11 terms allocated to equal-duration 40-year windows [5,6], years explicitly enumerated. Second is not an ordinal rank bar. Two tables, one flow and one geographic map also present. Brand Finance ranks 11/29/33/43 remain only in comparison table with explicit noncardinal survey interpretation.
producer_checks.bilingual_parity: 205 annual entries each; same 15 materially edited year-specific claims in both languages; paired evidence URLs identical, 2 quantitative count charts [1,2,2,0,1,2,1,1,1] [5,6], 2 tables, 1 flow and 1 map per language. Cross-language wordings equivalent.
producer_checks.editorial_status: Revision 7 staged following independent rev6 QA rejection for exactly 1997,2003,2007 source mismatches; no approval exists and no public report created. Awaiting independent review with SHA check.
